passages.t: The Word of life, heard, seen and touched
passages.happening:
The letter has no greeting. It begins straight away with what the writer and others saw.

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life. And this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us” (verses 1-2).

“We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ. We write these things so that our joy may be complete” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
The first readers would have heard an echo at once. John's Gospel begins, “In the beginning was the Word”. This letter begins with ‘that which was from the beginning’, and with ‘the Word of life’. The one who was with God from the start is the same one the witnesses knew.

Notice the verbs. Heard. Seen with our own eyes. Gazed upon. Touched with our own hands. In Greek the opening is one long, crowded sentence, piling up these words before it reaches its main verb, ‘we proclaim’. The word for ‘touched’ can mean to handle or feel for something. Luke uses it when the risen Jesus tells his disciples to touch him and see that he has flesh and bones (Luke 24:39).

Why stress the senses so much? Because some teachers had left these churches with a different account of Jesus. They seem to have said that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body, or that he came upon the man Jesus for a time and left him. Against that, John says: the eternal life of God was not a vision or an idea. It was a person who could be heard and seen and handled. And the ‘we’ of these verses are people who were there.

Then John says why he writes. It is not to win an argument. It is for fellowship. The Greek word is koinōnia, a partnership, a life held in common. Business partners had it, and so did friends who shared what they owned. John wants his readers to share the life that he and the other witnesses share, and that life is ‘with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ’. And when they share it, his own joy will be complete.
passages.ot:
John's first words reach back to the first words of the Bible: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The life that was ‘from the beginning’ belongs to God himself.

The psalms speak of God as the source of all life: “For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light” (Psalm 36:9). John says that this life has now been ‘revealed’ in a person.

And Israel knew the hope of God living among his people: “I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (Exodus 29:45). John's Gospel says that “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14); this letter says the witnesses touched him.
passages.asks: Ask what it means for you that the Christian faith rests on a real person whom people saw and touched, and not on an idea or a feeling. Ask whether your faith is something you hold alone, or a life you share with others. And ask whose joy would be more complete if you came closer to them, and to God.

passages.happening:
“And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (verse 5).

“If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
John gives the message in five words: ‘God is light’. Then he adds, ‘in Him there is no darkness at all’. God's goodness is complete. There is nothing mixed in it, nothing hidden, nothing false.

Light and darkness were strong pictures in the ancient world. Greek thinkers often used light for knowledge. The Dead Sea Scrolls, written by a Jewish group before and during the time of Jesus, speak of a struggle between ‘the sons of light’ and ‘the sons of darkness’. In the Old Testament, light stands for God's presence, his holiness and his truth. John's picture has a moral edge. To walk in darkness is to live in sin and falsehood.

Then comes the first of three claims John tests. ‘If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie.’ Someone may claim to know God while living as if he did not. John says such a claim is false. It is not only wrong words. It is not ‘practising’ the truth. Truth in this letter is something you do.

The other side is good news. If we walk in the light, two things follow. We have fellowship with one another; walking toward God brings believers toward each other. And ‘the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin’. Walking in the light does not mean we have no sin. It means we live in the open before God, where his cleansing goes on. And it is the blood of Jesus, a real death of a real man, that does it.
passages.ot:
‘God is light’ echoes the psalms: “The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 27:1).

The prophets pictured a day when God himself would be the light of his people: “for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor” (Isaiah 60:19).

And light was God's first word in creation: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3).

Cleansing by blood comes from Israel's sacrifices. On the Day of Atonement, the law said, “atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (Leviticus 16:30).
passages.asks: Ask where you are tempted to say one thing about God and live another. Ask what it would mean to walk ‘in the light’, with nothing hidden before him. And ask whom you are walking toward, and whom you are walking away from.

passages.t: If we say we have no sin
passages.happening:
“If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (verses 8-9).

“If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Two more claims, each tested. First: ‘we have no sin’. Some may have thought that their special knowledge put them above sin, or that what the body did did not touch the spirit. John says a person who claims this has fooled himself.

Second: ‘we have not sinned’. This goes further. It denies having done wrong at all. John says it makes God out to be a liar, because God's word says plainly that people sin and need forgiving.

Between the two claims stands the promise. ‘If we confess our sins.’ The word for confess means, literally, to say the same thing. To confess is to agree with God about our sin, to call it what he calls it. And when we do, God is ‘faithful and just to forgive’.

‘Faithful’ means he keeps his word. ‘Just’ is more surprising. One might expect a just God to punish, not forgive. But John has just spoken of the blood of Jesus. God's forgiveness is just because it rests on Christ's sacrifice, not on God pretending that sin does not matter. He forgives, and he does more: he cleanses ‘from all unrighteousness’.

Notice that the passage is honest and hopeful at once. The way out of sin is not to deny it, and not to despair over it. It is to bring it into the light.
passages.ot:
Confession was part of Israel's worship. On the Day of Atonement the high priest was to “confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:21).

The psalms show its relief: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and You forgave the guilt of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

The wisdom books say the same: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

And the psalms knew that no one stands without mercy: “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:3-4).
passages.hard:
If believers are already forgiven through Christ, why do they need to keep confessing their sins? And how does this fit with chapter 3, where John says that no one born of God keeps on sinning?

The question is fair. The New Testament teaches that those in Christ are justified once for all: “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Many Christians answer by telling apart a believer's standing before God and the daily relationship. Justification, God's declaring a sinner righteous through Christ, does not need to be repeated. But fellowship with God is harmed by sin, and confession restores it, much as a child who has wronged a parent is still a child but needs to set things right. Jesus taught his disciples to ask the Father for forgiveness as a regular part of prayer (Matthew 6:12).

Others say that verse 9 is not describing a new transaction each time. It describes the shape of the Christian life: those who walk in the light keep agreeing with God about their sin, and keep finding that his forgiveness holds. Either way, John's point is pastoral. The alternative to confession is not a higher spirituality. It is self-deception.

As for chapter 3, John is not contradicting himself. The note on 3:4-10 sets out the main ways Christians read the two passages together. On any reading, chapter 1 stands: anyone who says he has no sin is deceived. And chapter 2 begins with comfort for those who do sin: they have an advocate with the Father.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask which of the three claims you are most tempted to make: that you can know God and live in the dark, that you have no sin, or that you have not sinned. Ask what it would mean to agree with God about one thing in your life today. And ask whether you believe that he is faithful and just to forgive you.
